stimuli.title: A Spanish missionary's report to the Crown, 1540s (practice text)
stimuli.text: In the islands and on the mainland, the Spaniards who hold Indians in encomienda work them in the mines and the fields from dawn until night. They give them little food and no rest, and whole villages have died out. These people are Your Majesty's vassals and have souls to be saved. I beg that they be freed from such masters and taught the faith by gentle means, as the Church intends.

stimuli.title: A Virginia planter's letter to a London merchant, 1690s (practice text)
stimuli.text: Fewer servants come from England every year, and those who come expect land of their own when their terms end, though the best land near the rivers is already taken. Since the troubles in Bacon's time, many gentlemen here think it safer and cheaper in the end to buy Africans, who serve for life, as do their children. I have bought six this year and mean to plant more tobacco.

stimuli.title: A historian's interpretation (practice text)
stimuli.text: The exchange of plants, animals and germs between the hemispheres after 1492 reshaped both. Maize and potatoes from the Americas fed Europe's growing population, and horses brought by the Spanish transformed life on the Great Plains. Yet the heaviest consequence fell on the Americas, where smallpox, measles and other diseases killed a large majority of native people within a century of contact.

stimuli.title: A French missionary's account of New France, early 1700s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The French in Canada are few, and they live among the native nations as traders and allies. Our young men travel to the villages for furs, marry there and learn the languages, and the chiefs call the governor their father. The English, by contrast, come in great numbers, cut down the forests and fence the land for farms, so that the nations near them have no place left to hunt.

stimuli.title: A Spanish officer's report from New Mexico, 1680 (practice text)
stimuli.text: In August of this year the Pueblo Indians of every town rose together on the same day. They burned the churches, killed many of the friars and settlers, and drove the rest of us south to El Paso. Their leaders say they will no longer give up their old ceremonies or labor for the Spaniards, and they have returned to the ways of their ancestors.

stimuli.title: A Massachusetts minister's sermon, 1640s (practice text)
stimuli.text: We have entered into a covenant with God to build a commonwealth where His laws are honored. If we keep it, He will bless us; if we break it, all the world will see our shame. Let every family read the Scriptures, let every town keep a school, and let no man live idle or disturb the peace of the church with new opinions.

stimuli.title: A historian's interpretation (practice text)
stimuli.text: Before 1492, North America held hundreds of societies, each shaped by its environment. In the arid Southwest, peoples dug irrigation ditches to grow maize and built towns of stone and adobe. In the Northeast, villages mixed farming with hunting and fishing. On the Northwest coast, abundant salmon and forests supported large permanent villages with little farming at all.

stimuli.title: A New York lawyer's pamphlet, 1765 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The Parliament of Great Britain has laid a tax upon our newspapers, our deeds and our licenses. We do not deny the King's authority, nor the right of Parliament to regulate the trade of the empire. But we do deny that a body in which we have no voice may take our property without our consent. The rights of Englishmen were not left behind when our fathers crossed the ocean.

stimuli.title: A farmer's letter on the proposed Constitution, 1787 (practice text)
stimuli.text: This new government will reach into every county with its tax collectors and its courts. Where is the bill of rights to guard the press, the jury and the conscience? A single government over so wide a country, with a few representatives for many thousands of people, must end in the rule of the rich and well born. Let the states keep the power that is close to the people.

stimuli.title: A Republican newspaper editorial, 1798 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Congress has made it a crime to write anything false or scandalous against the President or the Congress, and the President may now expel any alien he judges dangerous. A printer who criticizes the government may be fined and jailed. Is this the liberty for which we fought eight years? The states must declare these laws void before every free press is silenced.

stimuli.title: A historian's interpretation (practice text)
stimuli.text: The Revolution's language of liberty reached beyond the men who wrote it. Some women argued that the new republic needed educated mothers to raise virtuous citizens, and northern states began to end slavery, most of them gradually. Yet slavery grew in the South, and women gained no vote anywhere except, for a time, in New Jersey.

stimuli.title: A Pennsylvania settler's complaint, 1764 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The King's proclamation forbids us to settle west of the mountains, on the very lands our militia fought the French and their Indian allies to win. The officers in London would keep the western nations quiet at our expense, and they send soldiers to guard the line who do nothing to protect our farms.

stimuli.title: A Massachusetts creditor's letter, 1787 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Armed farmers in the western counties have closed the courts to stop the collection of debts and taxes. Our state has raised men to put them down, but Congress has no money and no army to help. Unless the union is given more strength, every state will fall into such disorder, and our credit abroad will be lost.

stimuli.title: An American merchant's letter, 1793 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Now that France and Britain are at war again, some of our countrymen call on us to aid our old ally France. But our ships carry goods to both nations, and our young country has no navy to protect them. War would ruin our trade and perhaps the union itself. Let us be friends to all and allies to none.

stimuli.title: Enslaved population of the United States, census years (rounded)
stimuli.text:
| Census year | Enslaved people |
|---|---|
| 1800 | 0.9 million |
| 1820 | 1.5 million |
| 1840 | 2.5 million |

Note: Congress banned the importation of enslaved people into the United States from 1808.

stimuli.title: A letter from a young woman in a Massachusetts textile mill, 1845 (practice text)
stimuli.text: We are up before five and at the looms until seven in the evening, with half an hour for each meal. The wages let me send money home to help my brother at the academy, and I have savings of my own besides. But the company has cut our pay and given each girl a fourth loom to tend, and some of us talk of signing a petition to the legislature for a ten-hour day.

stimuli.title: A petition from Cherokee leaders to Congress, 1830s (practice text)
stimuli.text: We have adopted a written constitution, built schools, mills and farms, and printed a newspaper in our own language. The land on which we live is ours by treaties made with the United States. We ask only that those treaties be honored, and that we not be driven from the graves of our fathers to a strange country west of the Mississippi.

stimuli.title: An address by a reform society, 1830s (practice text)
stimuli.text: Every person may turn from sin and choose a better life. If that is so, then society too may be made new. Let us close the grog shops that ruin families, build common schools for every child, and care for the insane in hospitals instead of chaining them in jails. The work is God's, but the hands must be ours.

stimuli.title: A newspaper commentary on the President's message, 1823 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The President has told the powers of Europe that the American continents are no longer open to new colonies, and that any attempt to restore the old empires over the new republics of the south will be seen as unfriendly to the United States. In return, he promises that we will stay out of the quarrels of Europe.

stimuli.title: A Democratic newspaper editorial, 1832 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The President's veto strikes down a monster bank that serves the rich men of Philadelphia and foreign stockholders, a bank that no Congress should have chartered. The farmer and the mechanic have found a champion who will not let the money power rule the republic.

stimuli.title: A New York editorial, 1845 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Providence has given this continent to our growing people, and no foreign power has the right to block our spread from ocean to ocean. Texas has joined the Union; Oregon must follow, and the lands beyond will one day be ours as well. This is not conquest but the natural growth of a free nation.

stimuli.title: Two historians on the coming of the Civil War (practice texts)
stimuli.text:
**Historian A:** The war came because of slavery. Every crisis of the 1850s, from Kansas to the Dred Scott case, turned on whether slavery would spread into the West, and the states that seceded said plainly that they left the Union to protect it.

**Historian B:** The sectional crisis was also a failure of politics. After the Kansas-Nebraska Act, the Whig Party broke apart, and the new parties that rose in its place drew their votes from one section only. With no national party left but a divided Democracy, there was little room for the bargains that had settled earlier crises.

stimuli.title: A Freedmen's Bureau agent's report from South Carolina, 1866 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The freedpeople are eager for schools; old and young crowd into every room we open. Many wish to rent or buy land of their own, but the planters will not sell to them. The new state laws bind laborers to contracts for the whole year and punish any Black man found without work as a vagrant, so that many are forced back to the plantations on the old terms.

stimuli.title: An abolitionist newspaper, 1850 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Congress has passed a law that makes every northern citizen a slave catcher. A person claimed as a fugitive may not speak in his own defense, and the commissioner who hears the case is paid more for sending a person south than for setting him free. No free Black person in Boston or Philadelphia is safe.

stimuli.title: A Union official's report, 1863 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The war has been a school of national power. Congress has issued a national paper currency, chartered national banks, granted public lands to settlers who will farm them and to a company that will build a railroad to the Pacific, and raised the tariff to protect northern industry. None of this could have passed before the war.

stimuli.title: A Union soldier's letter home, 1863 (practice text)
stimuli.text: When I enlisted I fought only to save the Union. But I have seen the plantations now, and the slaves who come into our lines bring us news of the rebels and dig our earthworks. The President's proclamation makes this a war for freedom, and I believe it will weaken the rebels more than any battle.

stimuli.title: A congressman's speech, 1846 (practice text)
stimuli.text: If we win new land from Mexico, let it be free soil, open to the free white laborer and closed forever to slavery. I do not ask to touch slavery where it is. I ask only that the territory won by the blood of the whole nation not be given to the slaveholder.

stimuli.title: A northern newspaper, 1857 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The Court has ruled that Black Americans, free or enslaved, cannot be citizens, and that Congress has no power to bar slavery from any territory. If this is law, then the Missouri line was void all along, and no territory can be kept free. What is left of free soil?

stimuli.title: An industrialist's essay, 1889 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The concentration of business in the hands of a few is the law of progress. It has given us cheaper goods than any age before has known, and competition, hard as it is on some, ensures the survival of the fittest in every line of work. The man of wealth should regard himself as a trustee for the community and use his surplus during his own life to build libraries, parks and schools, rather than leave it to his heirs.

stimuli.title: A Kansas farmers' newspaper, 1891 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The railroads charge what they please to carry our grain, the banks hold our mortgages, and money grows scarcer every year while our crops fetch less. Both old parties serve the same masters. We demand that the government own the railroads, coin silver freely, and let the people elect their senators.

stimuli.title: European immigrants to the United States by region of origin (approximate, rounded shares)
stimuli.text:
| Region of origin | 1880s | 1900s |
|---|---|---|
| Northern and western Europe (such as Britain, Ireland, Germany, Scandinavia) | about 80% | about 25% |
| Southern and eastern Europe (such as Italy, Austria-Hungary, the Russian Empire) | about 20% | about 75% |

stimuli.title: A reformer's report on reservation policy, 1880s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The tribal system holds the Indian back. As long as land is held in common, no man has reason to improve it. If each family is given its own plot to farm, and the children are sent to boarding schools to learn English and a trade, the Indian will in one generation become a citizen like any other.

stimuli.title: A railroad car builder's statement during a strike, 1894 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The company cut our wages again this spring, but it did not lower the rents on the houses it owns in its town, where we must live. We walked out, and the railway union refused to handle the company's cars. Now the government has sent troops, and a federal court has ordered the union to stop the strike.

stimuli.title: A Black newspaper editor, 1896 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The Court now says that a state may require separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers so long as they are equal. Everyone knows they will never be equal. The law has given its blessing to the color line, and every state that wishes to draw it will do so.

stimuli.title: A Georgia newspaper editor's speech, 1886 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The old South rested on slavery and cotton alone. The new South will build mills beside its rivers and railroads across its fields, welcome northern capital, and teach its sons the trades of industry. We have buried the past and turned our faces to the future.

stimuli.title: A magazine article by a journalist, 1906 (practice text)
stimuli.text: In the packing houses, meat that had fallen on the floor among the sawdust was shoveled back into the hoppers, and spoiled hams were treated with chemicals and sold as fresh. The workers who handle the meat have no place to wash their hands. The public buys these products in good faith, trusting a label that no one checks.

stimuli.title: A speech by a member of the Anti-Imperialist League, 1899 (practice text)
stimuli.text: We went to war with Spain to free Cuba. Now we pay Spain for the Philippines and make war on the Filipinos, who want only a government of their own. A republic cannot rule subjects without their consent and remain a republic. If we hold these islands by force, we abandon the principles on which our own nation was founded.

stimuli.title: Two historians on the New Deal (practice texts)
stimuli.text:
**Historian A:** The New Deal saved American capitalism by reforming it. Deposit insurance ended the bank runs, new rules policed the stock market, and Social Security gave ordinary people a stake in the system, all without ending private ownership of business.

**Historian B:** The New Deal did less than it promised. Full recovery came only with spending for the Second World War, and programs such as Social Security at first left out farmworkers and domestic workers, groups that included a large share of Black workers.

stimuli.title: A letter from a Black migrant in Chicago to a friend in Mississippi, 1917 (practice text)
stimuli.text: I got work at the stockyards for more pay than I ever saw at home, and my children go to a school that is open all year. I voted in the city election last month, and nobody stood in my way. There is prejudice here too, and the rents are high, but a man can breathe. Tell your brother there are jobs for him if he will come.

stimuli.title: A socialist pamphlet, 1917 (practice text)
stimuli.text:
Do not submit to the draft. This war is fought for the profits of bankers and munition makers, and the working man of America has no quarrel with the working man of Germany. Stand up for your rights.

Note: The pamphlet's author was convicted under a new federal law passed after the United States entered the war.

stimuli.title: A Tennessee newspaper, 1925 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The trial in Dayton pits the old faith against the new science. A young teacher stands accused of teaching that man descended from lower forms of life, against the law of this state. Reporters have come from across the country, and the whole nation is listening on the radio.

stimuli.title: A woman working in an aircraft plant, 1943 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Two years ago I was a waitress earning tips. Now I rivet wings for bombers and earn more than my father did. My husband is in the Pacific, and my mother keeps the children. The foreman says we will go back home when the men return, but I am not so sure I want to.

stimuli.title: A State Department official's memo, 1947 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The Soviet Union will press outward wherever it finds weakness, but it will retreat before firm strength. Our answer must be steady, long-term containment: aid to free peoples resisting outside pressure, the rebuilding of Europe's economies, and military strength enough to make aggression unprofitable.

stimuli.title: A college student's statement, North Carolina, 1960 (practice text)
stimuli.text: We sat down at the lunch counter and asked to be served like any other customer. When they would not serve us, we stayed until closing, and the next day more of us came. We did not strike back when we were cursed or when food was poured on us. We mean to show the nation the wrong of segregation by our conduct.

stimuli.title: A campaign speech by a conservative candidate, 1980 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Washington has grown too big, too costly and too sure of itself. It taxes too much, spends too much and regulates too much. We will cut tax rates so working people keep more of what they earn, lift needless rules from business, and rebuild a defense that our adversaries will respect.

stimuli.title: A student newspaper editorial, 1968 (practice text)
stimuli.text: For two years the government told us the enemy was nearly beaten. Then came the attacks at the new year, in the cities that were supposed to be safe. We are told to fight a war that Congress has never declared, and our friends are drafted to fight it while the sons of the well connected find a way out.

stimuli.title: A magazine article, 1955 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Where potato fields stood eight years ago, thousands of nearly identical houses now line curving streets. Young veterans buy them with little money down through federally backed loans, then drive the new highways to jobs in the city. Every family seems to have a television, a car and children under ten.

stimuli.title: An economist's essay, 1999 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Trade barriers are falling around the world, and a factory in Ohio now competes with one in Mexico or China. Capital moves across borders in seconds. Personal computers and the internet are changing how Americans work, shop and learn, and the jobs that are growing demand more education than the ones that are disappearing.

stimuli.title: A speech by a federal official, 1965 (practice text)
stimuli.text: This year Congress has given us medical care for the elderly through Social Security and federal aid to the poorest schools, and last year it began job training for young people who have never held a job. We aim not merely to relieve poverty but to prevent it, and to build a society where no one is left out.

stimuli.title: A letter to a women's magazine, 1963 (practice text)
stimuli.text: I have a husband, three children and a new house with every appliance. I went to college. And still, as I make the beds and drive to the market, I ask myself whether this is the whole of my life. I suspect I am not the only woman in this neighborhood asking.

stimuli.title: A newspaper column, 2002 (practice text)
stimuli.text: After the attacks of last September, Congress gave investigators new powers to monitor communications and search records, and few members read the bill before voting. Security matters, but so does liberty. Every generation that has faced a war has had to decide how much freedom it will trade for safety.

questions.stem: The conditions described in the report were most directly a result of
options: English settlement along the Chesapeake Bay
competition between Spain and France over the fur trade
Spanish efforts to profit from forced native labor
the spread of the Protestant Reformation into Spain
questions.explanation: The encomienda system gave Spanish colonists the right to demand labor and tribute from native people, and it was used to work mines and plantations for profit. French fur trading and English settlement came later and elsewhere.

questions.stem: The missionary's argument most directly reflects
options: the view that land should be bought from native nations by treaty
debates in Spain over the moral treatment of native peoples
a Spanish policy of avoiding contact with native societies
support for replacing Catholic missions with trading posts
questions.explanation: Some Spanish clergy argued that native people were subjects of the Crown with souls to save and should not be brutalized, which fed a long debate in Spain over colonial labor. Spain sought contact and conversion, not separation.

questions.stem: Which development was most directly a response to the decline in native population described in the report?
options: The end of the casta system in New Spain
Growing imports of enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies
The rise of indentured servitude among New England fishing families
The founding of Jamestown as an English colony
questions.explanation: As disease and overwork killed native workers, Spanish colonists turned increasingly to enslaved Africans for labor in the Caribbean and elsewhere. The casta system of racial ranks lasted through the colonial era.

questions.stem: Which development most directly explains the shift in labor described in the letter?
options: The end of the Atlantic slave trade
The Great Awakening's challenge to the authority of the Anglican church
Parliament's passage of the Navigation Acts
Bacon's Rebellion and fewer English servants
questions.explanation: After Bacon's Rebellion in 1676, in which poor freedmen joined an uprising, and as fewer English servants arrived, Chesapeake planters relied more on enslaved Africans. The Navigation Acts regulated trade, not labor.

questions.stem: The letter best illustrates which trend in the Chesapeake colonies in the late 1600s?
options: Slavery becoming hereditary and based on race
The decline of tobacco as the region's main export
The spread of religious toleration laws to all colonies
The growth of an economy built on small farms and fishing
questions.explanation: The planter notes that Africans serve for life and so do their children: colonial laws in this era made slavery hereditary and tied it to race. Small farms and fishing describe New England.

questions.stem: Compared with the Chesapeake colonies, the New England colonies of the same era generally
options: depended more on enslaved labor in plantation agriculture
relied more on family farms, trade and free labor
grew more tobacco for export to England
had fewer towns, schools and churches
questions.explanation: New England's colder climate and rocky soil favored family farms, fishing, shipbuilding and trade, and its towns were organized around churches and schools. Tobacco and plantation slavery defined the Chesapeake.

questions.stem: A historian would find the letter most useful as evidence of
options: living conditions in West African societies
planters' reasons for their labor choices
the views of enslaved Africans about plantation work
official British policy toward the colonies
questions.explanation: The letter shows a planter's reasons for buying enslaved Africans, including the memory of Bacon's Rebellion. It cannot show what enslaved people themselves thought, since it is written by an enslaver.

questions.stem: The tax described in the pamphlet was part of
options: British efforts to pay debts from the Seven Years' War
Parliament's response to the Declaration of Independence
Congress's plan to fund the Louisiana Purchase
British plans after the defeat at Saratoga
questions.explanation: The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed printed papers to help pay for the war with France and the troops kept in North America afterward. The other events came later.

questions.stem: The author's main argument rests on the principle that
options: taxes require the people's consent
the King has no authority in America
colonists should pay more taxes than Britons
the colonies should declare independence at once
questions.explanation: The author accepts the King's authority and Parliament's power over trade but denies that Parliament, where colonists have no voice, may tax them. That is the principle of no taxation without representation.

questions.stem: Which colonial response most directly followed arguments like the author's?
options: Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts
Boycotts and the Stamp Act Congress
The Albany Plan of Union
The signing of the Treaty of Paris of 1763
questions.explanation: Colonists organized nonimportation agreements, and delegates from nine colonies met in the Stamp Act Congress to protest; Parliament repealed the act in 1766. The Albany Plan and the 1763 treaty came before.

questions.stem: Arguments like the author's were later developed most fully in
options: Washington's Farewell Address of 1796
the Northwest Ordinance
the Proclamation of 1763
the Declaration of Independence
questions.explanation: By 1776 colonial leaders moved from defending the rights of Englishmen to denying Parliament's authority entirely, and the Declaration listed taxation without consent among its grievances.

questions.stem: Concerns like the farmer's most directly led to
options: the Great Compromise on representation
the outbreak of the Whiskey Rebellion
the XYZ Affair with France
the Bill of Rights in 1791
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists demanded protections for the press, juries and conscience, and Federalists promised amendments to win ratification. The first ten amendments were ratified in 1791.

questions.stem: The farmer would most likely have supported
options: keeping most power in the state governments
a national executive with a longer term
abolishing the state governments
giving Congress power to tax imports and land directly
questions.explanation: The letter warns that a distant national government will rule for the rich and asks that the states keep their power. That was the Anti-Federalist position.

questions.stem: Which group was most likely to share the farmer's views?
options: Creditors who wanted protection for contracts
Small farmers in rural areas wary of distant power
Supporters of a strong national army
Merchants in port cities who wanted one trade policy
questions.explanation: Rural farmers far from the coast tended to oppose the Constitution, fearing taxes and courts run by distant elites. Merchants and creditors were mostly Federalists.

questions.stem: Which development most directly explains the growth shown in the table?
options: The growth of tobacco farming in New England
The reopening of the Atlantic slave trade to American ports after 1808
The spread of slavery into the Northwest Territory
The spread of cotton growing in the Deep South
questions.explanation: The cotton gin made short-staple cotton profitable, and cotton plantations spread across Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana, driving demand for enslaved labor. The slave trade stayed closed after 1808.

questions.stem: Given the note under the table, the growth after 1808 came mainly from
options: the arrival of free African immigrants
legal imports of enslaved people from the Caribbean
the enslavement of European immigrants
natural increase among people already enslaved
questions.explanation: With imports banned, the enslaved population grew mostly through births: enslaved people were born into slavery under hereditary laws. Some smuggling continued, but it was small by comparison.

questions.stem: The trend shown in the table most directly contributed to
options: the decline of southern power in the House
a sharp fall in cotton exports to the textile mills of Britain
a large domestic slave trade
the end of slavery in Virginia by 1840
questions.explanation: As cotton spread west, enslavers in Virginia and Maryland sold hundreds of thousands of people south and west, breaking up families. Cotton exports to Britain rose, not fell.

questions.stem: Which political conflict of the period was most directly tied to the trend in the table?
options: Jackson's war on the Second Bank
The crisis over admitting Missouri
The Hartford Convention of 1814
The Embargo Act of 1807
questions.explanation: Missouri's request to enter as a slave state raised the question of slavery's spread west and was settled by the Missouri Compromise. The bank, embargo and Hartford Convention turned on other issues.

questions.stem: The letter best reflects
options: early factory work in the market revolution
the decline of manufacturing in New England
the rise of sharecropping in the South
the spread of craft guilds that controlled wages in American towns
questions.explanation: Textile mills in Lowell and other New England towns hired young women from farm families, an early step in industrialization. Sharecropping came after the Civil War.

questions.stem: The petition for a ten-hour day is an example of
options: Populist demands for the free coinage of silver
the program of the American Federation of Labor
the temperance movement's goals
early organizing by industrial workers
questions.explanation: Lowell workers organized, struck over pay cuts and petitioned the legislature for shorter hours in the 1830s and 1840s. The AFL and the Populists came decades later.

questions.stem: Which development most directly made mills like this one possible?
options: The closing of the western frontier
Water power and new canals and railroads
The Homestead Act's grants of free land to factory workers
The repeal of the protective tariff
questions.explanation: Mills used river water power, and canals and early railroads carried raw cotton in and cloth out. The tariff in this period protected, rather than harmed, American textiles.

questions.stem: In the late 1840s and 1850s, mill owners increasingly replaced workers like the letter writer with
options: children brought from the Northwest Territory
Irish immigrants paid lower wages
Chinese immigrants from California
enslaved workers hired out by southern planters
questions.explanation: As famine drove Irish immigration in the late 1840s, mill owners hired Irish families at lower pay, and the share of New England farm women in the mills fell.

questions.stem: Which evidence would Historian A most likely use?
options: Secession declarations naming slavery
The Compromise of 1877
The Panic of 1873
The collapse of the Whig Party in the 1850s
questions.explanation: Historian A argues that slavery caused the war and that seceding states said so; several states' declarations of causes named slavery directly. The Whig collapse fits Historian B.

questions.stem: Which development best supports Historian B's argument?
options: A Republican Party with only northern support
The Gadsden Purchase
The Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 and its effect in Britain
Eli Whitney's cotton gin
questions.explanation: Historian B stresses parties that drew votes from one section. The Republican Party, formed in 1854, won almost no southern votes, and Lincoln won in 1860 without a single southern electoral vote.

questions.stem: Both historians would most likely agree that
options: the Compromise of 1850 ended the sectional crisis
conflict over the West deepened sectional division
slavery played little part in the politics of the 1850s
economic differences alone caused the war
questions.explanation: A points to Kansas and the territories; B starts the party collapse with the Kansas-Nebraska Act. Both see the question of the West as central to the breakdown.

questions.stem: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 raised tension because it
options: admitted California as a free state
required northern citizens to help return people who escaped slavery
banned slavery in every western territory
let settlers decide on slavery north of the 1820 line
questions.explanation: The act applied popular sovereignty to Kansas and Nebraska, effectively repealing the 1820 line, and pro- and antislavery settlers fought over Kansas. The fugitive slave law was part of 1850.

questions.stem: The "new state laws" in the report are best described as
options: the Reconstruction Amendments
Jim Crow laws upheld in Plessy v. Ferguson
the Homestead Act
Black Codes
questions.explanation: In 1865 and 1866 southern legislatures passed Black Codes that limited freedpeople's rights and forced them into labor contracts. Jim Crow segregation laws spread later in the century.

questions.stem: Congress responded to laws like these by
options: approving the Compromise of 1877
closing the Freedmen's Bureau at once and ending federal aid to freedpeople
repealing the Thirteenth Amendment
passing the Fourteenth Amendment and the Reconstruction Acts
questions.explanation: Republicans in Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1866, sent the Fourteenth Amendment to the states and, in the Reconstruction Acts of 1867, divided the South into military districts.

questions.stem: Because few freedpeople could obtain land, many came to work under
options: sharecropping
the putting-out system
the encomienda system
indentured servitude
questions.explanation: Sharecroppers farmed a planter's land for a share of the crop, a system that often trapped families in debt. Indentured servitude was a colonial labor system.

questions.stem: Reconstruction came to an end in 1877 most directly when
options: the Fifteenth Amendment was ratified
federal troops left the South after a disputed election
the Freedmen's Bureau was created
the House impeached Andrew Johnson for violating the Tenure of Office Act
questions.explanation: In the Compromise of 1877, Democrats accepted Rutherford B. Hayes as president and the last federal troops were withdrawn from the South, leaving the remaining Republican state governments to fall.

questions.stem: The essay's view of the duty of the rich is known as
options: the Populist platform
the Social Gospel
the Square Deal
the Gospel of Wealth
questions.explanation: Andrew Carnegie's idea that the wealthy should give away their fortunes for the public good during their lives was called the Gospel of Wealth. The Social Gospel called on churches to reform society.

questions.stem: The phrase "survival of the fittest" shows that the essay drew on
options: the ideal of republican motherhood
Social Darwinism
transcendentalist ideas about nature
Puritan ideas of a covenant community
questions.explanation: Social Darwinists applied ideas of natural selection to society, arguing that competition rewarded the most able and that the poor were less fit.

questions.stem: Critics of the essay's view of business would most likely have argued that
options: philanthropy should replace all government services
tariffs on imported goods were too low
big business harmed workers and small firms
factories should move from the North to the South
questions.explanation: Labor leaders, farmers and reformers argued that trusts used their power to cut wages, fix prices and drive out smaller firms.

questions.stem: Which federal law responded most directly to the concentration of business the essay defends?
options: The Homestead Act of 1862
The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890
The Pendleton Act of 1883
The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882
questions.explanation: The Sherman Act outlawed combinations in restraint of trade, though courts at first enforced it weakly and even used it against unions.

questions.stem: The demands in the newspaper are most closely associated with
options: the Whig Party
the Know-Nothing Party
the People's Party
the Federalist Party
questions.explanation: The People's Party, formed by farmers' alliances, called in its 1892 Omaha Platform for government ownership of railroads, free silver and direct election of senators.

questions.stem: The demand to "coin silver freely" was meant to
options: raise prices and ease farmers' debts
lower the tariff on imported goods
replace all paper money with gold
shrink the money supply to fight inflation
questions.explanation: Farmers suffered from falling prices; more money in circulation would raise crop prices and make debts easier to repay.

questions.stem: Which later reform achieved one of the newspaper's demands?
options: The Twenty-first Amendment's repeal of Prohibition
The Eighteenth Amendment's ban on alcohol
The Seventeenth Amendment's direct election of senators
The Nineteenth Amendment's guarantee of women's suffrage
questions.explanation: Progressives took up several Populist demands, and the Seventeenth Amendment of 1913 provided for the popular election of senators, who had been chosen by state legislatures.

questions.stem: Articles like this one led most directly to
options: two food safety laws in 1906
the Sherman Antitrust Act
the Federal Reserve Act
the Interstate Commerce Act
questions.explanation: Exposes of the meatpacking industry, above all Upton Sinclair's The Jungle, pushed Congress to pass both food safety laws in 1906. The Sherman and Interstate Commerce Acts came earlier.

questions.stem: Journalists who wrote articles like this one were known as
options: scalawags
Copperheads
muckrakers
Mugwumps
questions.explanation: Theodore Roosevelt gave investigative journalists the name muckrakers. Mugwumps were reform Republicans of the 1880s; Copperheads were antiwar Democrats in the Civil War.

questions.stem: The article reflects the Progressive belief that
options: only private charity should help consumers
the market would correct itself without regulation
government should protect consumers from business
states alone should set food safety rules
questions.explanation: Progressives argued that in an industrial economy, consumers and workers needed expert government regulation to protect them.

questions.stem: Which reform of the same era also aimed to make government more responsive to the public?
options: The spoils system in federal hiring
The initiative, referendum and recall
Poll taxes adopted across the South around 1900
Allotment of reservation land
questions.explanation: Progressives gave voters ways to propose laws, vote on them directly and remove officials. Southern poll taxes did the opposite, keeping Black and poor white citizens from voting.

questions.stem: The speech was a response to
options: the annexation of the Philippines
the building of the Panama Canal
the purchase of Alaska
the war with Mexico
questions.explanation: In the 1898 Treaty of Paris, Spain ceded the Philippines to the United States for a payment, and the Senate approved it in 1899 over the objections of anti-imperialists.

questions.stem: Supporters of annexation argued that
options: annexation would violate the Monroe Doctrine
the Philippines should be granted independence at once
the United States should leave the Pacific to Britain
the islands offered markets and naval bases
questions.explanation: Expansionists pointed to trade with China, coaling stations for the navy and a supposed duty to uplift Filipinos, an idea tied to the racial thinking of the time.

questions.stem: The speaker's argument relies most on
options: the Open Door notes on China
Social Darwinist ideas of racial competition
the Declaration's principle of consent
the Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine
questions.explanation: Anti-imperialists argued that ruling Filipinos without their consent contradicted the founding idea that governments derive their powers from the consent of the governed.

questions.stem: Which development followed the annexation the speaker opposed?
options: Immediate independence for the Philippines in 1899 under American protection
A war against Filipino independence fighters
Japanese control of the islands by 1900
Spain's recovery of the islands
questions.explanation: Filipinos who had fought Spain resisted American rule in the Philippine-American War, which lasted from 1899 into the early 1900s. Independence came in 1946.

questions.stem: The policy described in the memo was first applied in
options: the Truman Doctrine
the Good Neighbor policy toward Latin America
the Monroe Doctrine
the Neutrality Acts
questions.explanation: In 1947 Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey, pledging to support free peoples resisting outside pressure, the first statement of containment as policy.

questions.stem: Which event of 1948 and 1949 tested the policy in the memo in Germany?
options: The Bay of Pigs invasion
The Berlin Airlift
The Cuban Missile Crisis
The U-2 incident over the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: When the Soviets blockaded West Berlin in 1948, the United States and Britain supplied the city by air for almost a year until the blockade was lifted. The other crises came in 1960 to 1962.

questions.stem: Which alliance grew out of the policy in the memo?
options: The Triple Entente
The League of Nations
The Warsaw Pact
NATO
questions.explanation: In 1949 the United States joined NATO, its first peacetime military alliance, pledging to defend western Europe. The Warsaw Pact was the Soviet bloc's answer.

questions.stem: The policy in the memo later led most directly to
options: the Spanish-American War
the end of the Cold War in 1950
an American withdrawal from Europe
American wars in Korea and Vietnam
questions.explanation: Containment was extended to Asia, where the United States fought to stop communist advances in Korea from 1950 and in Vietnam in the 1960s and 1970s.

questions.stem: The students in the statement used
options: armed self-defense against attackers
a lawsuit in federal court
nonviolent direct action
a call for Black separatism
questions.explanation: The 1960 sit-ins, which began at a Woolworth's counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, used peaceful, disciplined protest to expose segregation.

questions.stem: Which organization grew directly out of protests like the one described?
options: The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee
The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People
The American Indian Movement
The Black Panther Party
questions.explanation: Student sit-in leaders founded SNCC in 1960 with the help of Ella Baker. The NAACP dated from 1909, and the Black Panthers from 1966.

questions.stem: When the Supreme Court upheld the 1964 federal ban on segregation in places such as restaurants and motels, it relied on Congress's power to
options: declare war and raise armies
enforce the Fifteenth Amendment
admit new states to the Union
regulate interstate commerce
questions.explanation: In Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964) the Court held that segregated hotels and restaurants burdened interstate travel and trade, so Congress could ban it under the commerce clause. The Fifteenth Amendment concerns voting.

questions.stem: The speech reflects
options: the Populist movement
the Progressive movement
the New Deal coalition
the rise of the new right
questions.explanation: A movement of tax cutters, anticommunists and religious conservatives grew from the 1960s and won the presidency in 1980, calling for smaller government.

questions.stem: Which policy followed most directly from ideas like those in the speech?
options: Federal ownership of the railroads and airlines
The creation of Medicare
Large cuts in income tax rates
Deep cuts in defense spending
questions.explanation: In 1981 Congress cut income tax rates sharply, while defense spending rose. Medicare was a Great Society program of 1965.

questions.stem: Which context helped the speech's message win support?
options: Inflation and distrust of government
The start of the Great Depression
The economic boom of the late 1990s
The fall of the Berlin Wall
questions.explanation: Stagflation, the energy crisis, Watergate and the Iran hostage crisis left many Americans distrustful of government and receptive to conservative arguments.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence would best support the historian's claim about the Great Plains?
options: The Plains became the center of English settlement
Plains peoples gave up hunting to grow sugar cane for export
Many Plains peoples hunted bison on horseback
Spanish missions replaced most Plains villages by 1550
questions.explanation: Horses spread north from Spanish colonies, and many Plains nations, such as the Comanche and Lakota, built mounted bison-hunting economies around them. Sugar cane was a Caribbean plantation crop.

questions.stem: The main reason disease spread so devastatingly in the Americas after 1492 was that
options: Europeans deliberately avoided contact with native towns and trade routes
native societies had no agriculture to feed the sick
native peoples had no immunity to Eurasian diseases
Spanish law required native people to live in cities
questions.explanation: Smallpox, measles and influenza had circulated in Eurasia for centuries but were new to the Americas, so native populations had no acquired immunity. Many native societies farmed extensively.

questions.stem: Which effect of the exchange on Europe is most consistent with the excerpt?
options: New American crops helped support population growth
European rulers lost interest in overseas colonies
Europe adopted the horse from the Americas
European diets became far less varied as American crops replaced wheat
questions.explanation: The historian notes that maize and potatoes from the Americas fed Europe's growing population. The horse moved the other way, from Europe to the Americas.

questions.stem: The differences the missionary describes are best explained by
options: French fur trading and English farming
the absence of Catholic missionaries in New France
English laws forbidding colonists to clear forest land
the French goal of building large tobacco plantations
questions.explanation: New France had few settlers and depended on the fur trade, which required native partners, while English colonies drew many settlers who wanted land to farm. Catholic missionaries were active in New France.

questions.stem: Which group would most likely have shared the missionary's view of the English colonists?
options: Native nations losing land to English farms
Investors in the Virginia Company of London
Members of the Virginia House of Burgesses seeking western land grants
Puritan leaders in Massachusetts Bay
questions.explanation: Native nations near the English colonies saw forests cleared and land fenced, which ended hunting there. Puritan leaders, burgesses and investors all supported English expansion.

questions.stem: The relationships described in the excerpt most directly contributed to
options: the end of the fur trade in North America
French alliances with native nations against Britain
the rapid growth of French cities on the Atlantic coast
a decline of Spanish missions in Florida and New Mexico
questions.explanation: Trade, marriage and diplomacy tied many native nations to the French, and they fought alongside France in the imperial wars, including the French and Indian War. The fur trade continued long afterward.

questions.stem: The missionary's purpose in contrasting the French and the English was most likely to
options: show French officials the value of native allies
describe Spanish methods of converting native peoples in the missions of Florida
argue that France should give up North America
recruit English farmers to settle in Canada
questions.explanation: By stressing how the French live among native nations as allies while the English drive them away, the writer argues that France's approach strengthens its position. Nothing suggests he wants France to leave.

questions.stem: The laws the editorial attacks were passed during
options: the ratification of the Articles of Confederation
the debate over the Missouri Compromise
the War of 1812 with Britain
party conflict during the Quasi-War with France
questions.explanation: In 1798, during an undeclared naval war with France, the Federalist Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts, which Republicans saw as aimed at them and their supporters.

questions.stem: Which response came from opponents of these laws?
options: The Judiciary Act of 1789
The Hartford Convention of New England Federalists
The Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions
Jay's Treaty with Britain
questions.explanation: Jefferson and Madison wrote resolutions for Kentucky and Virginia arguing that states could judge the acts unconstitutional. The Hartford Convention was a Federalist meeting during the War of 1812.

questions.stem: The editorial is evidence of which development of the 1790s?
options: The end of the first party system
The rise of opposing political parties
A decline in the political role of newspapers
Agreement among national leaders on foreign policy toward France
questions.explanation: Federalists and Democratic-Republicans divided over the national bank, France and Britain, and the limits of federal power, and partisan newspapers carried the fight.

questions.stem: In the 1790s, Democratic-Republicans like the editor generally favored
options: closer commercial ties with Britain through Jay's Treaty
strict construction and sympathy for France
a high protective tariff to build manufacturing
a national bank and a strong central government
questions.explanation: Jefferson's followers read federal powers narrowly and sympathized with revolutionary France. The national bank, ties with Britain and support for manufacturing were Federalist positions.

questions.stem: The idea that the republic needed educated mothers to raise virtuous citizens is usually called
options: the Half-Way Covenant
the cult of domesticity
the Second Great Awakening
republican motherhood
questions.explanation: Republican motherhood gave women a political role inside the home: raising sons for citizenship. The cult of domesticity is a later, nineteenth-century ideal of separate spheres.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence best supports the historian's claim about northern states?
options: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850
Pennsylvania's gradual abolition law of 1780
Eli Whitney's invention of the cotton gin in Georgia in 1793
The three-fifths clause of the Constitution
questions.explanation: Pennsylvania passed the first gradual abolition law in 1780, and other northern states followed. The three-fifths clause and the cotton gin strengthened slavery.

questions.stem: The historian's argument is best described as claiming that the Revolution
options: had no effect on ideas about rights
had limited and uneven effects
brought full political equality to women in every state
ended slavery throughout the new nation
questions.explanation: The excerpt credits the Revolution with new ideas about women and the start of northern emancipation, but stresses that slavery grew in the South and women did not gain the vote.

questions.stem: The petition was written in response to
options: the Indian Removal Act and Georgia's claims
the Northwest Ordinance
the Proclamation of 1763
the Dawes Act's division of reservation land into family plots
questions.explanation: In 1830 Congress passed the Indian Removal Act, and Georgia, eager for Cherokee land where gold had been found, extended its laws over the Cherokee Nation. The Dawes Act came in 1887.

questions.stem: The Cherokee leaders' strategy in the petition emphasized
options: a request to become citizens of Georgia under its state laws
a voluntary move to Indian Territory
armed resistance in alliance with Britain
treaty rights and new institutions
questions.explanation: The petition points to a written constitution, schools and a newspaper and to treaties with the United States: it argues through law and through institutions white Americans would recognize.

questions.stem: Which Supreme Court decision supported the Cherokee position?
options: Marbury v. Madison
McCulloch v. Maryland
Dred Scott v. Sandford
Worcester v. Georgia
questions.explanation: In Worcester v. Georgia (1832) the Court held that Georgia's laws had no force in the Cherokee Nation. McCulloch concerned the national bank; Marbury established judicial review.

questions.stem: Despite the petition and the Court's ruling, the result was
options: the return of Cherokee land taken by Georgia
a new treaty guaranteeing Cherokee land in Georgia
Cherokee citizenship in the state of Georgia
removal on the Trail of Tears
questions.explanation: The Jackson administration did not enforce the ruling, and after a treaty signed by a minority faction the army forced most Cherokee west in 1838 and 1839. Thousands died on the way.

questions.stem: The address reflects which religious idea of the period?
options: The Gospel of Wealth preached by industrialists
Social Darwinism
Puritan belief in predestination
The Second Great Awakening
questions.explanation: Revivalists of the Second Great Awakening taught that individuals could choose to be saved and could perfect themselves and society, which inspired many reform movements. Puritans believed God had already chosen the saved.

questions.stem: The call to care for the insane in hospitals is most closely linked to the work of
options: Frederick Douglass
Dorothea Dix
Horace Mann
Jane Addams
questions.explanation: Dorothea Dix documented the treatment of mentally ill people in jails and almshouses and persuaded states to build asylums. Horace Mann led the common school movement.

questions.stem: Which group was most active in reform societies like the one in the excerpt?
options: Southern planters and their families in the cotton states
Recent Irish Catholic immigrants
Middle-class women and men in the North
Western fur traders
questions.explanation: Reform societies drew heavily on northern middle-class Protestants, and women led and filled many of them. Many Irish Catholic immigrants resented temperance campaigns.

questions.stem: Many people active in reform societies of the 1830s also took part in
options: the Populist Party's campaign for free silver in the 1890s
abolitionism and women's rights
the Progressive Party of 1912
the Federalist Party
questions.explanation: The same networks of reformers, many of them women, worked against slavery and for women's rights; the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention grew partly out of abolitionist work.

questions.stem: The law described in the newspaper was part of
options: the Compromise of 1850
the Crittenden Compromise
the Kansas-Nebraska Act
the Missouri Compromise
questions.explanation: The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state and, to satisfy the South, included a much stronger fugitive slave law. The Crittenden plan of 1860 and 1861 was never adopted.

questions.stem: Many northerners responded to the law with
options: calls for the North to secede in 1850
an end to the Underground Railroad
new state constitutions that allowed slavery
personal liberty laws and antislavery votes
questions.explanation: Northern states passed personal liberty laws to hinder enforcement, crowds sometimes rescued captured fugitives, and many voters who had ignored slavery turned against the South.

questions.stem: Which work published soon after had a purpose most similar to the newspaper's?
options: Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin
Alexis de Tocqueville's Democracy in America
Thomas Paine's Common Sense
Upton Sinclair's The Jungle
questions.explanation: Stowe wrote her 1852 novel partly in protest against the Fugitive Slave Act, and it turned many northern readers against slavery. Common Sense argued for independence in 1776.

questions.stem: Defenders of the law in the South argued that it
options: would end slavery in the western territories won from Mexico
protected the rights of free Black northerners
enforced a duty set out in the Constitution
gave free states the right to decide on slavery
questions.explanation: The Constitution's fugitive slave clause required that people escaping service be delivered up, and southerners demanded that northern states honor it. They saw resistance to the law as a breach of the bargain of 1850.

questions.stem: The measures in the report could pass largely because
options: Britain lent the Union the money to pay for them
southern members had left Congress
the Confederacy agreed to them in a peace treaty
the Supreme Court ordered Congress to pass them
questions.explanation: Southern Democrats had blocked a homestead law, a northern railroad route and higher tariffs before the war. With them gone, Republicans passed their program.

questions.stem: The public lands "to settlers who will farm them" refers to
options: the Dawes Act of 1887
the Homestead Act of 1862
the Northwest Ordinance of 1787
the Indian Removal Act of 1830
questions.explanation: The Homestead Act offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and farmed it for five years. The Pacific Railway Act granted land to the railroad.

questions.stem: The report's claims best support the argument that the Civil War
options: returned most powers to the states
ended federal involvement in the economy
permanently weakened the national economy
expanded federal power
questions.explanation: A national currency, national banks, land grants and a protective tariff all showed Washington taking on economic powers it had not used before the war.

questions.stem: Which other wartime measure also expanded federal authority over citizens?
options: The repeal of the protective tariff
The first federal military draft
The Hartford Convention
Jackson's Specie Circular
questions.explanation: The Enrollment Act of 1863 created the first national draft, which sparked riots in New York City. The Hartford Convention and the Specie Circular date from earlier decades.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the change shown in the table?
options: Immigration from Europe stopped after the 1880s
In the 1900s most immigrants came from Britain and Germany
Southern and eastern Europeans were most immigrants in both decades
Southern and eastern Europe became the main source
questions.explanation: The share from southern and eastern Europe rose from about a fifth to about three quarters. The table gives shares, not totals, so it says nothing about immigration stopping.

questions.stem: Which factor most directly drew the immigrants shown in the table to the United States?
options: Recruitment into the Union army
Free reservation land under the Dawes Act
Jobs in expanding industries and cities
The California gold rush
questions.explanation: Most of these immigrants settled in industrial cities and worked in mills, mines, factories and construction. The gold rush and the Civil War came earlier.

questions.stem: The change shown in the table contributed most directly to
options: the repeal of all federal immigration laws
a decline in the population of American cities
the end of Catholic and Jewish immigration
nativist demands to restrict immigration
questions.explanation: Many native-born Americans saw the new immigrants, often Catholic or Jewish and poor, as a threat, and pressed for literacy tests and later the quota laws of the 1920s.

questions.stem: Settlement houses such as Hull House responded to immigration by
options: offering classes and services in immigrant neighborhoods
settling immigrant families on western homesteads
lobbying Congress to end immigration from Europe
recruiting immigrants as strikebreakers
questions.explanation: Settlement house workers, many of them college-educated women such as Jane Addams, lived in immigrant neighborhoods and ran kindergartens, English classes and health clinics.

questions.stem: The reformer's proposals were carried out most directly in
options: the Dawes Act of 1887
the Indian Removal Act of 1830
the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934
the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868
questions.explanation: The Dawes Act divided reservation land into individual allotments and offered citizenship to those who took them. The 1934 act reversed allotment.

questions.stem: A major result of the policy the reformer proposed was
options: a sharp rise in Native landholding
the restoration of tribal governments
the closing of all Indian boarding schools
a large loss of Native land
questions.explanation: Land left after allotment was declared surplus and sold, and many allotments were later lost, so Native landholding fell by about two thirds by 1934.

questions.stem: The reformer's goal is best described as
options: keeping Native nations apart from settlers
removing Native nations west of the Mississippi
assimilation into white American culture
strengthening tribal self-government
questions.explanation: Individual farms, English and boarding schools were all meant to replace Native cultures with white American ways. Removal west had been the policy of the 1830s.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports Historian A?
options: Unemployment that stayed high until the early 1940s
The creation of federal insurance for bank deposits
The Supreme Court striking down the NIRA
The migration of families from the Dust Bowl
questions.explanation: The FDIC, created in 1933, insured deposits and ended the waves of bank runs, a reform that kept banks private. Persistent unemployment would support Historian B.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports Historian B?
options: The Tennessee Valley Authority's power plants
The end of the banking panic in 1933
Unemployment fell sharply only with war spending
The Securities and Exchange Commission's new rules for stock trading
questions.explanation: Unemployment was still high in the late 1930s and dropped quickly only after defense spending surged around 1940 and 1941.

questions.stem: Both historians would most likely agree that the New Deal
options: expanded the federal role in the economy
abolished private ownership of banks
ended the Great Depression by 1935
had little effect on the banking system or on the stock market
questions.explanation: A credits federal programs with saving capitalism; B says they fell short. Both describe a federal government doing far more than before.

questions.stem: Critics on the left, such as Senator Huey Long, argued that the New Deal
options: should be struck down by the courts
gave too little attention to business
did not redistribute enough wealth
spent far too much on relief
questions.explanation: Long's Share Our Wealth plan called for heavy taxes on great fortunes to give every family a basic income. Conservatives attacked spending and federal power.

questions.stem: The letter is evidence of
options: a return of Black northerners to the South
the Exodusters' move to Kansas in the 1870s
the Dust Bowl migration to California
the Great Migration
questions.explanation: From about 1915, hundreds of thousands of Black southerners moved to cities such as Chicago, Detroit and New York, and millions more followed over the next decades.

questions.stem: The movement described in the letter was encouraged most by
options: wartime labor shortages in the North
the end of segregation in the South
federal homestead grants in the North
new limits on Black voting in northern cities such as Chicago
questions.explanation: World War I cut off European immigration and raised demand for workers, so northern industries recruited Black southerners, who also sought to escape Jim Crow and violence.

questions.stem: Which event is the best evidence that there was "prejudice here too"?
options: The Harlem Renaissance
The Brown v. Board of Education decision
The Montgomery bus boycott
The Chicago race riot of 1919
questions.explanation: In the summer of 1919, white mobs attacked Black neighborhoods in Chicago and other cities as competition for jobs and housing grew. Montgomery and Brown came in the 1950s.

questions.stem: A cultural result of the movement described in the letter was
options: the Hudson River School
transcendentalism
the Harlem Renaissance
the Beat movement
questions.explanation: Black writers, artists and musicians gathered in Harlem in the 1920s, and figures such as Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston celebrated Black life and culture.

questions.stem: The "attacks at the new year" in the editorial refers to
options: the Bay of Pigs invasion
the Tet Offensive
the Berlin Airlift
the attack on Pearl Harbor
questions.explanation: In early 1968, during the Vietnamese new year, North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces attacked cities across South Vietnam. Though they were driven back, the offensive shook American confidence.

questions.stem: The claim that the war was never declared reflects that
options: the United Nations declared war on North Vietnam
Congress authorized force without a declaration
Congress declared war on North Vietnam in 1964
no American troops were in Vietnam before 1968
questions.explanation: In 1964 Congress gave President Johnson broad power to use force in Southeast Asia, but it never formally declared war.

questions.stem: Congress later tried to limit the president's power to wage undeclared wars with
options: the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s
the National Security Act of 1947
the War Powers Resolution of 1973
the Twenty-second Amendment
questions.explanation: The War Powers Resolution requires the president to notify Congress when sending troops into combat and limits how long they can stay without approval.

questions.stem: President Nixon responded to opposition like the editorial's mainly with
options: the containment policy of the Truman Doctrine
Vietnamization of the ground war
an immediate withdrawal of all troops in 1969
a large increase in the number of American troops
questions.explanation: Nixon withdrew American troops gradually while training and arming South Vietnam's army, though he also widened the bombing. The last combat troops left in 1973.

questions.stem: The "federally backed loans" in the article came most directly from
options: the Dawes Act
the Works Progress Administration of the 1930s
the Homestead Act
the GI Bill and federal mortgage insurance
questions.explanation: The GI Bill of 1944 gave veterans low-cost home loans, and federal mortgage insurance let buyers put little money down, fueling the suburban boom.

questions.stem: Which group was largely shut out of suburbs like the one described?
options: Black families
Factory workers with steady jobs
Veterans of World War II
Young married couples
questions.explanation: Developers often refused to sell to Black buyers, and federal lending rules and redlining denied loans in Black neighborhoods, so many suburbs were almost entirely white.

questions.stem: The suburban growth described in the article contributed most directly to
options: the growth of streetcar lines in new suburbs
a sharp drop in car ownership
a loss of people and tax revenue in many central cities
a fall in the birth rate during the 1950s
questions.explanation: As mostly white, middle-class families moved out, many older cities lost residents, businesses and tax money, while the baby boom kept the birth rate high and cars replaced streetcars.

questions.stem: The falling trade barriers the economist mentions include agreements such as
options: the Marshall Plan
NAFTA
the Embargo Act
the Smoot-Hawley Tariff
questions.explanation: NAFTA, in effect from 1994, removed most tariffs among the United States, Canada and Mexico. Smoot-Hawley raised tariffs in 1930.

questions.stem: Which development is most consistent with the trends the economist describes?
options: Growth of manufacturing's share of American jobs
Factory job losses in the Midwest
A decline in computer use at work
An end to immigration from Mexico
questions.explanation: As firms moved production abroad and automated, industrial towns in the Midwest and Northeast lost factory jobs, while service and technology jobs grew.

questions.stem: The trends described in the essay took place in the context of
options: the First World War
the Great Depression
the end of the Cold War
the rise of the Populist movement
questions.explanation: The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 opened new markets, and trade and investment across borders grew rapidly through the 1990s.

questions.stem: The uprising described in the report was most directly caused by
options: English colonists seizing Pueblo farmland
French traders selling guns to the Pueblos
Spanish suppression of Pueblo religion
a smallpox epidemic carried by Dutch sailors
questions.explanation: Spanish friars banned Pueblo ceremonies and colonists demanded labor and tribute, and the rebels said they would return to their own ways. There were no English settlers in New Mexico.

questions.stem: When the Spanish returned to New Mexico in the 1690s, they
options: handed the region to England by treaty
joined the Pueblos with the Iroquois Confederacy
gave up all claims north of Mexico permanently
tolerated more Pueblo customs
questions.explanation: After the revolt, returning Spanish authorities did not restore the encomienda and tolerated more Pueblo religious practice, a shift toward accommodation. Spain kept New Mexico until Mexican independence.

questions.stem: The revolt is most similar in cause to which conflict in the English colonies?
options: The Stono Rebellion of enslaved people in South Carolina
The Salem witch trials of 1692
Metacom's War in New England
The Glorious Revolution in England
questions.explanation: Metacom's War (King Philip's War, 1675 to 1676) was a native uprising against colonists who took land and pressed their ways on native peoples, much like the Pueblo Revolt. The Stono Rebellion was a revolt of enslaved Africans.

questions.stem: The sermon best reflects
options: the Puritan goal of a godly community bound by covenant
Enlightenment arguments for separating church and state
the Quaker belief in an inner light in every person
the Chesapeake focus on profit from tobacco
questions.explanation: Puritans saw their colony as a covenant community whose success depended on obeying God's laws. Quakers stressed an inner light and tolerance; Enlightenment thinkers later argued for separating church and state.

questions.stem: Which practice in New England followed most directly from ideas like those in the sermon?
options: Laws guaranteeing full religious freedom
Town schools teaching children to read the Bible
Royal governors appointing the minister of every Massachusetts town
Large plantations worked by enslaved laborers
questions.explanation: Because Puritans believed everyone should read Scripture, Massachusetts required towns to keep schools. Puritan colonies did not grant religious freedom; they punished dissenters.

questions.stem: Which development most directly challenged the authority of the minister in the sermon?
options: The dissent of Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson
The founding of Harvard College
The arrival of the Great Migration of Puritan families
The growth of town meetings
questions.explanation: Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson questioned the Puritan leaders' authority over conscience and were banished, the kind of new opinions the sermon warns against. Harvard and the Great Migration strengthened Puritan New England.

questions.stem: A century later, the authority of established ministers like this one was weakened most by
options: the passage of the Navigation Acts
the Proclamation of 1763
the First Great Awakening's preachers
the Albany Plan of Union
questions.explanation: In the 1730s and 1740s, itinerant revivalists such as George Whitefield urged a personal, emotional faith and split many congregations, undercutting settled ministers. The Albany Plan and Proclamation were political.

questions.stem: The excerpt best supports which claim?
options: Native societies adapted to their environments
Maize was unknown north of Mexico before 1492
Every native society depended mainly on hunting
Most native societies were nomadic before 1492
questions.explanation: The historian shows irrigation farming in the Southwest, mixed farming in the Northeast and fishing villages on the Northwest coast, each suited to its region. Southwest peoples grew maize, so maize was known north of Mexico.

questions.stem: The spread of maize cultivation into the Southwest most directly encouraged
options: a shift to herding cattle
the domestication of the horse
trade with European merchants
irrigated, settled towns
questions.explanation: Maize farming in a dry climate required irrigation and supported permanent towns such as those of the ancestral Pueblo peoples. Horses and cattle arrived only with the Spanish.

questions.stem: The description of the Northwest coast challenges which assumption?
options: That Southwest peoples grew maize
That permanent villages required farming
That fishing mattered to coastal peoples
That native peoples traded with their neighbors along the coast
questions.explanation: Northwest coast peoples built large permanent villages on salmon and forest resources with little agriculture, so settled life did not always depend on farming.

questions.stem: England's Navigation Acts of the later 1600s were intended mainly to
options: raise revenue to pay for the Seven Years' War
encourage colonists to trade freely with Spain
keep colonial trade within the empire
end the Atlantic slave trade
questions.explanation: Mercantilist laws required certain colonial goods to be shipped to England on English or colonial ships, so the empire kept the profits. The Seven Years' War came much later, in the 1750s and 1760s.

questions.stem: The Middle Passage refers to
options: the canoe route of French fur traders along the Great Lakes
the forced voyage of captive Africans to the Americas
the overland route from Missouri to Oregon
the sea lane between England and New England
questions.explanation: The Middle Passage was the middle leg of the Atlantic trade, in which captive Africans were shipped in brutal conditions to the Americas, and many died on the way.

questions.stem: Which feature most distinguished the Middle Colonies, such as Pennsylvania and New York?
options: Very few towns or seaports
A single established church in every colony
An economy built on rice and indigo plantations
Diverse settlers and grain-exporting farms
questions.explanation: Settlers from many European backgrounds and faiths lived in the Middle Colonies, which exported wheat and flour through Philadelphia and New York. Rice and indigo were Lower South crops.

questions.stem: The British government issued the proclamation mainly to
options: raise money by taxing land sales west of the Appalachian Mountains
open the Ohio Valley to French traders
avoid new wars with western native nations
reward colonists for their service in the war
questions.explanation: After the war, native nations led by Pontiac attacked British forts, and Britain drew a line along the Appalachians to keep settlers apart from them and avoid costly wars.

questions.stem: The complaint best illustrates
options: colonial support for tighter British control
a return to Britain's earlier salutary neglect
colonial resentment of British policy
the end of conflict between settlers and native nations
questions.explanation: After 1763 Britain tightened control over the colonies with the proclamation, new taxes and troops, and colonists who had fought for the West resented it. Salutary neglect was the policy that ended.

questions.stem: Which earlier event set the stage for the settler's complaint?
options: The Boston Tea Party
Britain's victory in the Seven Years' War
The Glorious Revolution in England
The founding of the Georgia colony as a buffer against Spain
questions.explanation: The war removed France from North America east of the Mississippi and opened the question of who would control the western lands. The Tea Party came later, in 1773.

questions.stem: A similar tension between western settlers and eastern authorities appeared later in
options: the Seneca Falls Convention
the strikes at the Lowell mills
the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794
the Hartford Convention of 1814
questions.explanation: Western Pennsylvania farmers rose against a federal tax on whiskey, again resenting distant authorities who seemed to ignore frontier needs. The Hartford Convention was a New England Federalist meeting.

questions.stem: The uprising described in the letter is known as
options: the Whiskey Rebellion
Shays' Rebellion
the Stono Rebellion
Bacon's Rebellion
questions.explanation: In 1786 and 1787 indebted farmers in western Massachusetts, led in part by Daniel Shays, closed courts to stop foreclosures. The Whiskey Rebellion was in Pennsylvania in 1794.

questions.stem: Views like the creditor's most directly strengthened support for
options: a convention to revise the Articles
an alliance with Britain against the rebellious farmers
repealing the state constitutions
giving each state the power to coin money
questions.explanation: Fear of disorder after Shays' Rebellion convinced many leaders that the national government needed more power, and the convention that met in Philadelphia in 1787 wrote a new constitution.

questions.stem: The creditor's worry that "our credit abroad will be lost" most directly reflects which problem of the 1780s?
options: High tariffs that Congress set on imports
British taxes still collected in the states
Unpaid war debts owed to foreign lenders
A surplus in the national treasury
questions.explanation: The Confederation owed large sums to French and Dutch lenders from the war but, with no power to tax, could not even pay the interest. Congress had no power to set tariffs, and British taxes ended with independence.

questions.stem: The merchant's view matches which policy?
options: The Monroe Doctrine
Jefferson's Embargo Act cutting off foreign trade
Washington's Proclamation of Neutrality
The Alien and Sedition Acts
questions.explanation: In 1793 Washington declared the United States neutral in the war between France and Britain, despite the 1778 alliance with France. The Embargo Act of 1807 cut off trade altogether.

questions.stem: Which group would most likely have disagreed with the merchant?
options: New England shipowners
Supporters of Alexander Hamilton
Federalist merchants who traded with Britain
Democratic-Republicans who admired France
questions.explanation: Jefferson's supporters felt the United States owed France for its help in the Revolution and admired the French cause. Federalists and merchants favored peace and trade with Britain.

questions.stem: The merchant's advice was echoed a few years later in
options: the declaration of war against Britain in 1812
the Proclamation of 1763
