the Treaty of Alliance with France of 1778
Washington's Farewell Address
questions.explanation: In 1796 Washington urged the nation to avoid permanent alliances and stay out of European quarrels, the same caution the merchant expresses. The 1778 treaty came before.

questions.stem: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 was significant because it
options: set a path to statehood and banned slavery there
replaced the Articles of Confederation with a stronger union
opened the Louisiana Territory to settlement
created the first national bank
questions.explanation: The ordinance set out how the lands north of the Ohio River would be governed and admitted as equal states, and it banned slavery in that territory. Louisiana was purchased in 1803.

questions.stem: At the Constitutional Convention, the three-fifths compromise settled
options: how many senators each state would have in Congress
whether voters would elect the president directly
whether the Constitution would include a bill of rights
how enslaved people would count for representation and taxes
questions.explanation: Southern delegates wanted enslaved people counted for seats in the House; northern delegates objected. They agreed to count three fifths of the enslaved population for both representation and direct taxes.

questions.stem: Alexander Hamilton's financial plan included
options: an end to all tariffs on imports
repaying the national debt in paper money issued by the states
the sale of western lands only to small farmers
assumption of state debts and a national bank
questions.explanation: Hamilton proposed that the federal government take over the states' Revolutionary War debts, charter a national bank and raise revenue through tariffs and excise taxes, all to build national credit.

questions.stem: The policy described in the commentary is
options: the Open Door policy
the Monroe Doctrine
the Roosevelt Corollary
the Good Neighbor policy
questions.explanation: In 1823 President Monroe declared the Americas closed to new European colonization and promised that the United States would stay out of European affairs.

questions.stem: The policy was announced in the context of
options: Latin American wars of independence
the purchase of Alaska from Russia
the French invasion of Mexico during the American Civil War
the Spanish-American War
questions.explanation: Most of Spain's American colonies won independence in the 1810s and 1820s, and American leaders feared European powers might help Spain win them back.

questions.stem: At the time it was announced, the policy depended in practice on the navy of
options: Spain
France
Russia, which then held Alaska
Britain
questions.explanation: The United States had a small navy in 1823; Britain, which wanted open trade with Latin America, had the fleet that could actually keep other European powers out.

questions.stem: Later presidents expanded this policy most directly in
options: the Marshall Plan for Europe
the Neutrality Acts passed by Congress in the 1930s
the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904
the Washington Naval Conference
questions.explanation: In 1904 Theodore Roosevelt added that the United States could act as an international police power in the Western Hemisphere, turning a warning to Europe into a claim to intervene.

questions.stem: The editorial praises
options: Jackson's support for nullification in South Carolina
the creation of the Federal Reserve
the founding of Hamilton's First Bank of the United States
Jackson's veto of the bank recharter
questions.explanation: In 1832 Andrew Jackson vetoed the bill to recharter the Second Bank, calling it a privileged monopoly. He opposed nullification, and the Federal Reserve came in 1913.

questions.stem: The Whig Party opposed Jackson partly because Whigs
options: wanted to end every tariff
supported Indian removal more strongly
opposed any federal role in building roads, canals and banks
favored a national bank and internal improvements
questions.explanation: Whigs backed Henry Clay's American System: a national bank, protective tariffs and federally funded roads and canals. Jacksonian Democrats were the ones wary of federal economic power.

questions.stem: The editorial's appeal to farmers and mechanics reflects
options: the extension of the vote to women
a decline of mass political parties
equal voting rights for free Black men across the North
the expansion of voting rights to most white men
questions.explanation: By the 1820s and 1830s most states had dropped property requirements for white men, and parties competed for these new voters. Many states at the same time restricted voting by free Black men.

questions.stem: The idea in the editorial is known as
options: nullification
manifest destiny
republican motherhood
popular sovereignty
questions.explanation: The belief that the United States was destined by Providence to spread across the continent was called manifest destiny, a term coined in 1845.

questions.stem: Which event followed most directly from the views in the editorial?
options: The purchase of Florida from Spain
The Louisiana Purchase
The War of 1812
War with Mexico beginning in 1846
questions.explanation: Texas annexation and President Polk's push for California led to war with Mexico in 1846, which ended with the Mexican Cession in 1848. Louisiana and Florida were acquired earlier.

questions.stem: Whig critics of expansion in the 1840s argued that taking land from Mexico would
options: close the West to American settlers
end the cotton economy of the South
provoke a war with Britain over Florida
extend slavery and divide the nation
questions.explanation: Many Whigs, including a young Abraham Lincoln, opposed the war and warned that new territory would reopen the fight over slavery's spread, as it did.

questions.stem: Chief Justice John Marshall's rulings, such as McCulloch v. Maryland, generally
options: limited the Court's power of judicial review
strengthened federal power over the states
supported state laws removing native nations
let states tax federal institutions
questions.explanation: Marshall's Court upheld the national bank, barred states from taxing it and read the commerce power broadly, building federal authority. Worcester v. Georgia went against Georgia's removal laws.

questions.stem: The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, most directly
options: linked the Mississippi River with the Pacific Ocean by water
ended the need for railroads in the South
cut shipping costs from the Great Lakes to New York
carried southern cotton to New England mills
questions.explanation: The canal joined Lake Erie to the Hudson River, so western farm goods could reach New York City cheaply, and the city became the nation's leading port.

questions.stem: The Seneca Falls Convention of 1848 is best known for
options: launching the national temperance movement
founding the American Anti-Slavery Society in Boston
creating the first national labor union
a declaration of women's rights
questions.explanation: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott and others issued a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence that called for women's rights, including suffrage.

questions.stem: The proclamation the soldier mentions is
options: the Proclamation of Neutrality
the Ten Percent Plan
the Emancipation Proclamation
the Proclamation of 1763
questions.explanation: Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863. The Ten Percent Plan, announced later that year, set terms for southern states to rejoin the Union.

questions.stem: Lincoln justified the proclamation legally as
options: a war measure under his power as commander in chief
a treaty signed with the loyal border states
an act of Congress passed under the Thirteenth Amendment
a ruling of the Supreme Court in a wartime case
questions.explanation: Lincoln issued the proclamation as a military necessity under his war powers, which is why it applied only to areas in rebellion and why a constitutional amendment was later needed to end slavery everywhere.

questions.stem: Another effect of the proclamation was to
options: return escaped slaves to loyal owners
give women the vote in federal elections
open the Union army to Black men
end the Union blockade of southern ports
questions.explanation: The proclamation allowed Black men to serve, and about 180,000 served in the Union army, many of them formerly enslaved.

questions.stem: Slavery was abolished throughout the United States by
options: the Civil Rights Act of 1866
the Thirteenth Amendment
the Fourteenth Amendment
the Fifteenth Amendment
questions.explanation: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in 1865, abolished slavery except as punishment for a crime. The Fourteenth defined citizenship and equal protection; the Fifteenth protected voting.

questions.stem: The proposal in the speech is known as
options: the Freeport Doctrine
the Ostend Manifesto
the Crittenden Compromise
the Wilmot Proviso
questions.explanation: In 1846 Representative David Wilmot proposed banning slavery from any land taken from Mexico. It passed the House but failed in the Senate.

questions.stem: The speaker's appeal to "the free white laborer" reflects
options: nativist hostility to Catholic immigrants from Ireland and Germany
southern arguments for expanding slavery
free-soil ideas about protecting white workers
abolitionist demands for racial equality
questions.explanation: Free-soilers objected to slavery in the territories mainly because it would shut out free white farmers and workers, not because they sought equality for Black Americans.

questions.stem: Ideas like the speaker's led most directly to
options: the Hartford Convention
the founding of the Free Soil Party
the end of the Second Party System in 1828
the founding of the Populist Party
questions.explanation: Antislavery Whigs, Democrats and Liberty Party members formed the Free Soil Party in 1848 on the principle of no slavery in the territories; the Republicans later took up the same cause.

questions.stem: The case described in the newspaper is
options: Dred Scott v. Sandford
Plessy v. Ferguson
Gibbons v. Ogden
Cherokee Nation v. Georgia
questions.explanation: In 1857 Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled that Black Americans could not be citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories.

questions.stem: The ruling most alarmed Republicans because it
options: required states to let Black men vote
gave Congress the power to end slavery in the states where it already existed
undercut their goal for the territories
struck down the Fugitive Slave Act
questions.explanation: The Republican Party was built on stopping slavery's spread into the territories, and the Court said Congress had no such power.

questions.stem: Stephen Douglas tried to reconcile the ruling with popular sovereignty in
options: the Ostend Manifesto
the Wilmot Proviso
the Gettysburg Address
the Freeport Doctrine
questions.explanation: At Freeport in 1858, Douglas said settlers could still keep slavery out by refusing to pass laws to protect it. The answer cost him southern support in 1860.

questions.stem: The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, prohibited
options: literacy tests for voters in the South
poll taxes in federal elections
denying the vote on account of race
denying the vote on account of sex
questions.explanation: The amendment barred racial discrimination in voting, but it left room for poll taxes and literacy tests, which southern states later used to disenfranchise Black voters. Women's suffrage came in 1920.

questions.stem: Radical Republicans in Congress differed from President Andrew Johnson mainly over
options: whether to keep a protective tariff
whether to buy Alaska from Russia
how far to protect freedpeople's rights
whether to keep fighting the war in 1865 until the South surrendered unconditionally
questions.explanation: Johnson pardoned many Confederates and accepted the Black Codes; Radicals wanted civil and political rights for freedpeople and federal power to protect them.

questions.stem: California's request to enter the Union as a free state in 1849 and 1850 caused a crisis because it
options: required repealing the Missouri Compromise
would end the gold rush
would hand the Pacific coast back to Mexico under the treaty
would upset the Senate's sectional balance
questions.explanation: Admitting California would give the free states a Senate majority, so southern leaders demanded concessions, and Congress produced the Compromise of 1850.

questions.stem: The strike described in the statement is
options: the Homestead Strike
the Pullman Strike
the Great Railroad Strike of 1877
the Haymarket affair
questions.explanation: Workers at the Pullman Palace Car Company, who lived in the company town, struck in 1894 over wage cuts, and the American Railway Union boycotted Pullman cars. The Homestead Strike was at a steel mill in 1892.

questions.stem: The government's response described in the statement shows
options: federal support for workers' right to bargain
the government's neutrality in labor disputes between unions and railroads
a state law requiring an eight-hour day
federal use of troops and injunctions against strikes
questions.explanation: President Cleveland sent troops, saying the strike blocked the mail, and a federal court issued an injunction against the union. Protection for collective bargaining came only in the 1930s.

questions.stem: The union that joined the strike was
options: the Knights of Labor led by Terence Powderly
the American Railway Union led by Eugene Debs
the Industrial Workers of the World
the American Federation of Labor led by Samuel Gompers
questions.explanation: Eugene Debs's American Railway Union organized all railroad workers in one union. Debs was jailed after the strike and later became a Socialist leader. The IWW was founded in 1905.

questions.stem: Labor unions of this era struggled to win strikes mainly because
options: courts and governments backed employers
most factories were small family shops
most industrial workers already earned high wages
few immigrants worked in industry
questions.explanation: Employers could call on injunctions, state militias and federal troops, and they had a steady supply of new workers. Wages for unskilled industrial workers were low.

questions.stem: The editor is reacting to the decision in
options: Dred Scott v. Sandford
Worcester v. Georgia
Plessy v. Ferguson
Brown v. Board of Education
questions.explanation: In 1896 the Court upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars, holding that separate facilities were lawful if equal. Brown overturned that doctrine for schools in 1954.

questions.stem: The doctrine the editor criticizes is
options: separate but equal
judicial review
nullification
popular sovereignty
questions.explanation: Plessy established separate but equal, which southern states used to segregate schools, transport and public places for decades.

questions.stem: Which Black leader of the time urged Black southerners to focus first on vocational education and economic progress?
options: Booker T. Washington
Ida B. Wells
Marcus Garvey
W.E.B. Du Bois of the Niagara Movement
questions.explanation: Washington, head of the Tuskegee Institute, argued in his 1895 Atlanta speech for economic self-help before demands for equal rights. Du Bois rejected that approach and called for full civil rights.

questions.stem: The speech promotes
options: the free coinage of silver
a Populist alliance of Black and white farmers
the New South vision of industrial growth
a return to plantation slavery
questions.explanation: New South boosters wanted the South to industrialize with northern investment, building textile mills, railroads and iron works.

questions.stem: Despite hopes like the editor's, most of the South by 1900
options: remained mostly agricultural and poor
had become the center of national steel production
had ended the sharecropping system
had more factories than New England
questions.explanation: Some mills and iron works grew, but most southerners still farmed, many as sharecroppers or tenants, and the region's income lagged far behind the North's.

questions.stem: Which industry grew the most in the South in the decades after the speech?
options: Cotton textile mills
Automobile manufacturing
Shipbuilding on the Great Lakes
Aircraft building
questions.explanation: Textile mills spread across the Piedmont of the Carolinas and Georgia, drawing on cheap cotton, water power and low-wage labor. Autos and aircraft came in the twentieth century.

questions.stem: The Pendleton Civil Service Act of 1883 aimed to
options: fill some federal jobs by merit exams
regulate interstate railroad rates through a federal commission
restrict immigration from China
break up railroad monopolies
questions.explanation: After a disappointed office seeker assassinated President Garfield, Congress created a civil service commission and merit exams for some federal jobs, limiting the spoils system.

questions.stem: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was the first federal law to
options: limit immigration from all of Europe
grant citizenship to Chinese railroad workers
bar immigration of a group by nationality
end contract labor from Canada
questions.explanation: The act suspended immigration of Chinese laborers and was renewed until 1943, the first law to exclude a national group.

questions.stem: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887
options: paid for the first transcontinental railroad with federal bonds
broke up the Standard Oil trust
created a commission to oversee railroad rates
set a national minimum wage
questions.explanation: The act required railroad rates to be reasonable and created the Interstate Commerce Commission, the first federal regulatory agency, though it was weak at first.

questions.stem: The author of the pamphlet was most likely convicted under
options: the Espionage Act
the Alien and Sedition Acts
the PATRIOT Act
the Smith Act
questions.explanation: The Espionage Act of 1917 punished interfering with the draft, and the Sedition Act of 1918 extended it to criticism of the war effort. The Smith Act dates from 1940.

questions.stem: In a case about a similar pamphlet, the Supreme Court upheld such convictions using
options: the reasoning of Korematsu v. United States
the exclusionary rule in Mapp v. Ohio
the reasoning of Schenck v. United States
the right to counsel in Gideon v. Wainwright
questions.explanation: In Schenck (1919), Justice Holmes wrote that speech creating a clear and present danger, such as obstructing the draft in wartime, could be punished.

questions.stem: The pamphlet's view of the war was shared most by
options: the Committee on Public Information
most members of Congress in April 1917
socialists and pacifists
President Wilson's cabinet
questions.explanation: The Socialist Party opposed the war, and some pacifists did too. Congress voted for war by large margins, and the Committee on Public Information produced pro-war propaganda.

questions.stem: After the war, fear of radicals like the pamphlet's author led to
options: the Marshall Plan
the Neutrality Acts
the first Red Scare
the McCarthy hearings in the Senate
questions.explanation: Strikes, bombings and the Russian Revolution set off the Red Scare of 1919 and 1920, when Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer's agents arrested thousands of suspected radicals.

questions.stem: The trial described in the newspaper is
options: the trial of Eugene Debs
the Scopes trial
the Sacco and Vanzetti trial
the Haymarket trial
questions.explanation: John Scopes was tried in Dayton, Tennessee, in 1925 for teaching evolution, with William Jennings Bryan helping the prosecution and Clarence Darrow for the defense.

questions.stem: The trial reflected a broader conflict in the 1920s between
options: supporters and opponents of the gold standard
modernism and religious fundamentalism
farmers and railroads over freight rates
labor unions and coal mine owners
questions.explanation: The 1920s saw sharp clashes between modern, urban values and traditional, rural and religious ones, over evolution, Prohibition and immigration.

questions.stem: Which other development of the 1920s also reflected that cultural conflict?
options: The revival of the Ku Klux Klan
The Seneca Falls Convention
The First Great Awakening
The founding of the Populist Party
questions.explanation: The Klan of the 1920s, strong in the Midwest as well as the South, attacked immigrants, Catholics, Jews and Black Americans in the name of traditional values.

questions.stem: The worker's account best illustrates
options: the passage of the Nineteenth Amendment
women leaving paid work during the Depression
the nineteenth-century ideal of separate spheres
women's entry into war industries
questions.explanation: With millions of men in uniform, war industries hired women for skilled factory jobs, and the number of women in the workforce rose sharply.

questions.stem: Which other wartime change also brought new workers into American industry and farming?
options: A fall in federal spending
The Bracero Program for Mexican workers
An end to rationing of food and gasoline
Japanese Americans moving freely along the West Coast
questions.explanation: From 1942 the Bracero Program brought Mexican workers to farms and railroads. Japanese Americans on the West Coast were forced into camps, and rationing continued through the war.

questions.stem: During the same war, the federal government treated Japanese Americans on the West Coast by
options: granting them land in Hawaii
exempting them from all wartime laws
forcing them into camps
drafting them only into the navy
questions.explanation: Executive Order 9066 led to the removal and incarceration of about 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, and the Court upheld it in 1944.

questions.stem: In 1917, suffragists led by Alice Paul pressed for a constitutional amendment by
options: marching armed on the state capitol in Albany
picketing the White House during the war
sitting in at segregated lunch counters
boycotting the buses of several large cities
questions.explanation: Paul's National Woman's Party picketed the White House, and many were jailed; their pressure and women's war work helped win the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920. Sit-ins and bus boycotts belong to the civil rights movement.

questions.stem: Secretary of State John Hay's Open Door notes of 1899 and 1900 sought
options: the annexation of Chinese ports by the United States navy
Japan's opening to Western trade
an end to immigration from China
equal trading rights in China
questions.explanation: Hay asked the powers with spheres of influence in China to keep trade open to all and to respect China's territorial integrity. Japan had been opened to trade in the 1850s.

questions.stem: The Immigration Act of 1924
options: set national quotas that favored northern Europe
replaced national quotas with a system of family preferences
ended all limits on immigration from Asia
admitted refugees from Nazi Germany
questions.explanation: The act based quotas on the 1890 census, favoring northern and western Europe, and barred most Asian immigration. National quotas were replaced in 1965.

questions.stem: The programs in the speech were part of
options: the New Deal
John F. Kennedy's New Frontier
the Great Society
the Square Deal
questions.explanation: President Lyndon Johnson's Great Society included Medicare, Medicaid, federal aid to education and the War on Poverty. The New Frontier was Kennedy's program.

questions.stem: The "medical care for the elderly" in the speech is
options: the Affordable Care Act
the Social Security Act of 1935
Medicare
the GI Bill
questions.explanation: Medicare, created in 1965 as part of Social Security, provides health insurance for Americans 65 and older. Medicaid, created at the same time, covers many low-income people.

questions.stem: The speech reflects the belief that
options: the market alone would end poverty
the federal government should fight poverty
states should stop all aid to the poor
only private charity should help the poor
questions.explanation: Johnson's programs rested on the liberal view that federal action could end poverty and widen opportunity.

questions.stem: The programs in the speech were limited most by the cost of
options: the Korean War
the Marshall Plan
the Spanish-American War
the war in Vietnam
questions.explanation: As the Vietnam War grew in the late 1960s, it drew money and attention away from the War on Poverty.

questions.stem: The letter echoes the argument of
options: Upton Sinclair's The Jungle
Rachel Carson's Silent Spring
Michael Harrington's The Other America
Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique
questions.explanation: Friedan's 1963 book described the problem that has no name: educated suburban women unsatisfied by lives limited to home and family. Silent Spring was about pesticides.

questions.stem: Which organization, founded in 1966, worked for the kind of change the letter hints at?
options: The National Organization for Women
The AFL-CIO
The National American Woman Suffrage Association
The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee
questions.explanation: Friedan and others founded NOW to fight sex discrimination in jobs, education and law. The suffrage association had won its goal in 1920.

questions.stem: Which proposed amendment, backed by the women's movement, fell short of ratification?
options: The Twenty-fourth Amendment
The Nineteenth Amendment
The Equal Rights Amendment
The Twenty-sixth Amendment
questions.explanation: Congress passed the ERA in 1972, but opposition led by Phyllis Schlafly and others stopped it short of the 38 states needed by the deadline.

questions.stem: The law the column describes is
options: the Espionage Act
the War Powers Resolution
the USA PATRIOT Act
the Smith Act
questions.explanation: Passed weeks after the September 11, 2001, attacks, the PATRIOT Act expanded government surveillance and investigative powers.

questions.stem: The column's concern is most similar to
options: the free silver campaign of the 1890s
the fight over the national bank in the 1830s
debates over the tariff in the 1820s
civil liberties debates in earlier wars
questions.explanation: From the Sedition Act of 1798 to the Espionage Act and Japanese American incarceration, Americans have argued over how far wartime security may limit liberty.

questions.stem: Which military response followed the attacks the column mentions?
options: The Spanish-American War
The Korean War
The Persian Gulf War of 1991
Wars in Afghanistan and Iraq
questions.explanation: The United States invaded Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003 as part of what it called the war on terror. The Persian Gulf War came a decade earlier.

questions.stem: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Supreme Court
options: struck down poll taxes in state elections
upheld the doctrine of separate but equal
required busing of students between city and suburban districts
ruled that school segregation was unconstitutional
questions.explanation: The Court held unanimously that separate schools were inherently unequal, overturning Plessy for public education. Many southern states resisted for years.

questions.stem: The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962
options: began the American war in Korea
brought the superpowers close to nuclear war
led directly to the Bay of Pigs invasion by Cuban exiles
ended with an American invasion of Cuba
questions.explanation: Kennedy blockaded Cuba after spy planes found Soviet missile sites, and the Soviets removed them in exchange for a pledge not to invade Cuba. The Bay of Pigs came a year earlier.

questions.stem: Which development most changed the population of the United States in the decades after 1980?
options: Migration from the Sun Belt to the Rust Belt
A fall in immigration to almost none
Immigration from Latin America and Asia
Rising immigration mainly from northern Europe
questions.explanation: After the 1965 law ended national quotas, immigration rose, mostly from Latin America and Asia. Meanwhile Americans moved toward the Sun Belt, not away from it.
